kp: Workflows versus agents: choosing the right architecture
subject: eecs
stem: A team must build a feature that runs the same three fixed steps on every input — extract fields, validate them, then render a report — with no variation between runs. Which architecture fits best?
options: A workflow, since the steps are predictable and decomposable, giving better latency, cost, and determinism
An autonomous agent, so the model decides the steps on each run
A single agent with a large tool allowlist and no defined steps
Extended thinking with a large budget and no orchestration
explain: Predictable, decomposable tasks with fixed steps fit a workflow, which is cheaper and more deterministic than an agent. An agent adds nondeterminism the fixed task does not need, an undirected agent is the same mistake, and extended thinking does not orchestrate a multi-step pipeline.

kp: Workflows versus agents: choosing the right architecture
subject: eecs
stem: An engineer needs a system that debugs arbitrary failing tests, where the next action depends on what the previous step uncovered and cannot be scripted ahead of time. Which architecture fits best?
options: An agent, since the task is open-ended and its steps cannot be predicted in advance
A prompt-chaining workflow with all steps fixed up front
A single LLM call with no tools
A routing workflow that picks one of three fixed branches
explain: Open-ended tasks whose steps cannot be predicted fit an agent that directs its own tool use. A fixed chain or a preset routing workflow cannot express steps that depend on discoveries, and a single call has no tools to investigate.

kp: Workflows versus agents: choosing the right architecture
subject: eecs
stem: Following the principle of preferring the simplest thing that works, how should architecture escalate as a task's needs grow?
options: A single LLM call first, then a workflow, then an agent
An agent first, then a workflow, then a single call
Always start with a multi-agent system for maximum flexibility
A workflow first, then a single call, then extended thinking
explain: Prefer a single LLM call, then a workflow, then an agent, adding autonomy only when needed since it costs latency, spend, and determinism. Starting with an agent or a multi-agent system pays for complexity you may not need.

kp: Workflows versus agents: choosing the right architecture
subject: eecs
stem: What is the defining difference between a workflow and an agent?
options: In a workflow your code decides the steps through predefined paths; in an agent the model dynamically directs its own tool use
A workflow uses tools and an agent never does
An agent is always a single LLM call while a workflow is always many
A workflow can only run locally while an agent runs in the cloud
explain: The dividing line is who decides the steps: predefined code paths (workflow) versus the model directing its own control flow (agent). Both may use tools and multiple calls, and neither is defined by where it runs.

kp: Workflows versus agents: choosing the right architecture
subject: eecs
stem: Which of the following is a recognized workflow pattern for orchestrating LLM calls?
options: Orchestrator-workers, where a lead call splits a task and delegates subtasks
Backpropagation across the prompt tokens
Gradient routing of the attention heads
A single stateless call with no code around it
explain: Orchestrator-workers is a standard workflow pattern, alongside prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, and evaluator-optimizer. The others are not orchestration patterns — two are invented training-time terms and one is just a bare call.

kp: Parallel tool calls and multi-turn tool chaining
subject: eecs
stem: An assistant turn emits three tool_use blocks at once. How must your code return the results?
options: One tool_result per tool_use block, each carrying its matching tool_use_id, all in the next user message
A single combined tool_result summarizing all three, in the next assistant message
Three tool_result blocks spread one per turn over the next three messages
The results in strict call order, since the ids are ignored
explain: Return one tool_result per tool_use block, each tagged with its tool_use_id, all in the next user message; order does not matter as long as the ids match. Combining them, splitting them across turns, or relying on order instead of ids all break the pairing.

kp: Parallel tool calls and multi-turn tool chaining
subject: eecs
stem: You return two tool_result blocks but swap which tool_use_id each one carries. What happens?
options: The model associates each result with the wrong call, because results are matched to calls by tool_use_id, not by position
Nothing changes, since results are matched by their position in the array
The API rejects the turn because results must be in call order
The model reruns both tools automatically to recover
explain: Results are paired to calls by tool_use_id, so swapping ids makes the model read each result against the wrong call. Position does not determine the match, and the API does not auto-correct or rerun for you.

kp: Parallel tool calls and multi-turn tool chaining
subject: eecs
stem: Three independent read-only lookups have no dependency on one another. What is the most efficient way to run them?
options: Emit all three tool_use blocks in a single assistant turn so they run in parallel
Chain them across three turns, one lookup per turn
Merge them into one tool that cannot be reused elsewhere
Set disable_parallel_tool_use so they run one at a time
explain: Independent calls should be emitted together in one turn to parallelize and cut latency. Chaining serializes them needlessly, over-merging hurts reuse, and disabling parallel tool use is exactly the wrong move for independent reads.

kp: Parallel tool calls and multi-turn tool chaining
subject: eecs
stem: A task must first look up a user id, then load that user's orders using the id. Why can these two calls not be parallelized?
options: The second call depends on the first call's output, so it must be chained sequentially across turns
The API caps every turn at one tool call
Read tools can never run in parallel, only write tools can
Parallel calls are only allowed inside extended thinking
explain: Chaining is required when one tool's output feeds the next, so the order is forced by the data dependency. There is no one-call cap, reads can run in parallel when independent, and parallelism is unrelated to extended thinking.

kp: Parallel tool calls and multi-turn tool chaining
subject: eecs
stem: When is it appropriate to set disable_parallel_tool_use?
options: When you need calls to run one at a time in strict order rather than concurrently
When you want to speed up several independent reads
Whenever extended thinking is enabled
To force the model to always call at least three tools
explain: disable_parallel_tool_use forces one call at a time, which helps when strict ordering matters. It would slow independent reads (the opposite of the goal), is not tied to extended thinking, and does not set a minimum number of calls.

kp: Agent evaluation and observability
subject: eecs
stem: An agent produces open-ended written summaries that have no single correct answer. What is the most appropriate way to evaluate them at scale?
options: An LLM-as-judge scoring each summary against a written rubric
An exact string match against one gold summary
Manually reading a couple of outputs and shipping if they look fine
Counting output tokens and passing anything under a threshold
explain: Open-ended outputs are best graded by an LLM judge against a rubric, since there is no single correct string. Exact match fails when many phrasings are valid, eyeballing a few does not scale or catch regressions, and token count is not a quality measure.

kp: Agent evaluation and observability
subject: eecs
stem: An agent answers questions that each have a checkable, exact correct answer. Which grading method fits best?
options: Code-graded checks that compare the answer against the known correct value
An LLM-as-judge with a loose rubric, since judges are always preferable
A human reviewer for every single response in production
No grading, since exact-answer tasks can be trusted
explain: Where answers are checkable, code-graded evaluation is the most reliable and cheapest. A judge adds cost and noise when an exact check exists, per-response human review does not scale, and skipping evaluation forgoes any signal.

kp: Agent evaluation and observability
subject: eecs
stem: Before building an agent, why define success criteria for each task first?
options: Without a defined target you cannot tell whether a later change helped or hurt
Success criteria are only needed after the agent has shipped
They remove the need for any tracing or logging
They are required by the API before you can call tools
explain: Defining success up front (exact answers, rubric grades, pass rates) gives a baseline to measure changes against. They are needed before iterating, do not substitute for tracing, and are not an API prerequisite.

kp: Agent evaluation and observability
subject: eecs
stem: An agent occasionally runs many more loop iterations than expected and costs spike. Which observability practice most directly helps you diagnose it?
options: Logging each step's prompts, tool calls and results, stop_reason, and token usage
Lowering the temperature and hoping the loops stop
Turning off tool use entirely
Recording only the final answer, not the intermediate steps
explain: Step-level traces (prompts, tool calls and results, stop_reason, usage) show where and why the loop ran long and where cost accrued. Temperature is unrelated, disabling tools defeats the agent, and logging only the final answer hides the loop.

kp: Agent evaluation and observability
subject: eecs
stem: Which pair of signals works well as ongoing health metrics for a production agent?
options: Tool-call error rates and loop iteration counts
The character count of the system prompt and its file size
The model's parameter count and its release date
How many emojis appear in the output
explain: Tool-call error rate and loop iteration count are practical health signals that surface trouble early. Prompt size, model metadata, and emoji counts say nothing about whether the agent is behaving correctly.

kp: MCP resources, prompts, and sampling
subject: eecs
stem: An MCP server needs to summarize data using an LLM but has no API key of its own. Which MCP capability lets it do this?
options: Sampling — the server asks the client to run an LLM completion on its behalf
Resources — the server attaches files for the model to read
A tool call the server makes to itself
A user-invoked prompt template
explain: Sampling lets a server request an LLM completion from the client, so it can use AI without its own key, and the client (with optional human approval) stays in control. Resources attach context, servers do not call their own tools this way, and prompts are user-invoked templates.

kp: MCP resources, prompts, and sampling
subject: eecs
stem: With MCP sampling, who runs the actual LLM completion and keeps control over it?
options: The client, which the server asks to perform the completion and can gate with a human
The server, using its own separately configured API key
The tool itself, autonomously and without oversight
The user, who must type the completion by hand
explain: In sampling the client performs the completion at the server's request, keeping control and allowing a human in the loop. The server does not use its own key, the tool does not act autonomously, and the user does not write the completion manually.

kp: MCP resources, prompts, and sampling
subject: eecs
stem: In MCP, which primitive is model-controlled — invoked when Claude decides to?
options: Tools
Resources
Prompts
Transports
explain: Tools are model-controlled: the model decides when to call them. Resources are application-controlled context, prompts are user-controlled templates, and a transport is the connection channel, not a primitive the model invokes.

kp: MCP resources, prompts, and sampling
subject: eecs
stem: A host application attaches the currently open file to the conversation as context. Which MCP primitive is this, and who controls it?
options: A resource, which is application-controlled
A tool, which is model-controlled
A prompt, which is user-controlled
A sampling request, which is server-controlled
explain: Resources are application-controlled context, such as files or data the host attaches. Tools are model-controlled, prompts are user-controlled, and sampling is a server request the client fulfills — none of which match app-attached context.

kp: MCP resources, prompts, and sampling
subject: eecs
stem: A server exposes a reusable changelog template that the user triggers like a slash command. Which MCP primitive is this?
options: A prompt, which is user-controlled
A tool, which is model-controlled
A resource, which is application-controlled
A transport definition
explain: Prompts are user-controlled templates surfaced like slash commands. Tools are chosen by the model, resources are attached by the application, and a transport is the connection layer, not a template.

kp: Tool results engineering: size, format, pagination
subject: eecs
stem: A tool can return thousands of matching rows. What is the best way to shape its results for an agent?
options: Return one page of items plus a cursor or next-page token so the model can request more
Return all thousands of rows at once so nothing is missed
Return only a count, with no items or ids
Stream the raw database dump into the context
explain: Paginating with a page plus a cursor keeps result size bounded while letting the model fetch more on demand. Returning everything floods the context, a bare count is not actionable, and dumping raw data starves the loop.

kp: Tool results engineering: size, format, pagination
subject: eecs
stem: Why does a paginated tool result include a cursor or next-page token rather than just the first page?
options: So the model can ask for the next page on demand instead of receiving the whole list at once
Because cursors encrypt the results for security
Because the API forbids returning more than one item per call
So the results are automatically sorted alphabetically
explain: A cursor lets the model continue retrieval only when it needs more, keeping context small. Cursors are not an encryption feature, there is no one-item cap, and a cursor does not sort results.

kp: Tool results engineering: size, format, pagination
subject: eecs
stem: A single tool call returns 50K tokens of raw logs every time it runs. What is the main problem?
options: It consumes the context budget and is resent each turn, starving the rest of the loop
It makes the model respond in the wrong language
It disables prompt caching permanently
It changes the stop_reason to max_tokens on every call
explain: Large results are appended and resent each turn, eating the context budget and crowding out reasoning room. It does not affect output language, does not permanently disable caching, and does not set the stop_reason.

kp: Tool results engineering: size, format, pagination
subject: eecs
stem: Why should a list-returning tool include a stable id with each item?
options: So a follow-up call can fetch full detail for a chosen item on demand
So the model can sort the items by id length
Because ids remove any need for pagination
So the results can never be cached
explain: Stable ids let the model send a compact list first and hydrate only the items it needs via a follow-up call. Ids are not for sorting by length, do not replace pagination, and have nothing to do with disabling caching.

kp: Tool results engineering: size, format, pagination
subject: eecs
stem: How should verbose server-side logs be handled before being returned as a tool result?
options: Summarize or truncate them server-side and return only decision-relevant fields
Return them verbatim so the model has everything
Base64-encode the full logs to save space
Split them across ten tool calls with no summary
explain: Summarizing or truncating server-side and returning only decision-relevant fields keeps results compact. Returning everything floods context, base64 makes it larger and unreadable, and splitting raw logs across calls still dumps the same volume.

kp: Subagents and custom agent types in Claude Code
subject: eecs
stem: How do you define a custom subagent in Claude Code?
options: A Markdown file in .claude/agents/ with frontmatter for name, description, and tools
A JSON entry inside .mcp.json at the repo root
A shell script registered as a PreToolUse hook
A block appended to the user's shell profile
explain: Subagents are Markdown files in .claude/agents/ whose frontmatter sets name, description, and tools, and Claude delegates when the description matches. They are not defined in .mcp.json, as a hook, or in a shell profile.

kp: Subagents and custom agent types in Claude Code
subject: eecs
stem: In a subagent definition file, what does the description field control?
options: When Claude delegates to that subagent — it is matched against the task
The exact tokens the subagent must output
The network port the subagent listens on
The model temperature for the whole session
explain: The description is what Claude matches a task against to decide whether to delegate to the subagent. It does not fix output tokens, open a network port, or set session temperature.

kp: Subagents and custom agent types in Claude Code
subject: eecs
stem: Which statement best describes a Claude Code subagent?
options: A separate Claude instance with its own context window, system prompt, and tool allowlist
A second copy of the main context that shares its window
A plugin that runs inside the main agent's token budget
A cron job that restarts the CLI on a schedule
explain: A subagent is an isolated instance with its own context, prompt, and tool allowlist. It does not share the main window or token budget, and it is not a scheduler.

kp: Subagents and custom agent types in Claude Code
subject: eecs
stem: What is a primary benefit of delegating bulky work to a subagent?
options: Context isolation — the subagent works in its own window and returns only a summary
It guarantees the task finishes in a single tool call
It removes the need for any tool allowlist
It streams every intermediate token back into the main context
explain: Subagents isolate context: they do heavy work in their own window and hand back a summary, keeping the main context clean, plus tool scoping and parallelism. They do not guarantee one-call completion, still use an allowlist, and deliberately do not stream every token back.

kp: Subagents and custom agent types in Claude Code
subject: eecs
stem: A project defines a subagent named reviewer in .claude/agents/, and the user has a different reviewer in their home .claude/agents/. Which one is used?
options: The project agent — project scope overrides a user agent of the same name
The user agent — user scope always wins
Both run and their outputs are merged
Neither runs until the conflict is resolved by hand
explain: A project agent overrides a user agent of the same name, matching the settings hierarchy where project scope beats user. User scope does not win, the two are not merged, and no manual resolution is required.

kp: Project MCP servers and configuration scopes
subject: eecs
stem: The same MCP server name is configured at local, project, and user scope. Which configuration takes effect?
options: The local one — precedence runs local over project over user
The user one, since user settings are the broadest
The project one, because it lives in git
All three are merged field by field
explain: Precedence is local over project over user, so the local definition wins. User is the broadest but lowest priority, being in git does not grant precedence, and the scopes are not field-merged.

kp: Project MCP servers and configuration scopes
subject: eecs
stem: Between a project-scope server and a user-scope server of the same name, which one wins?
options: The project-scope server, since project overrides user in precedence
The user-scope server, since it applies across all projects
Whichever was configured most recently
They alternate on each session
explain: Project scope overrides user scope for the same name. Applying across projects does not raise user's priority, precedence is not decided by recency, and it does not alternate.

kp: Project MCP servers and configuration scopes
subject: eecs
stem: Which scope makes an MCP server private to you within a single project?
options: Local scope
Project scope
User scope
Enterprise scope
explain: Local scope is private to you in that one project. Project scope is shared with the team, user scope spans all your projects, and MCP server scopes do not include an enterprise tier here.

kp: Project MCP servers and configuration scopes
subject: eecs
stem: A team wants every member to get the same MCP servers automatically when they clone the repo. What should they do?
options: Define the servers in .mcp.json checked into the repo (project scope)
Add them at user scope on the team lead's machine only
Put them in local scope in each person's project
Paste the server config into the README as text
explain: Project scope means committing .mcp.json to the repo, so everyone who clones gets the servers. User scope stays on one machine, local scope is per-person and not shared, and README text is not loaded as configuration.

kp: Project MCP servers and configuration scopes
subject: eecs
stem: How should a committed .mcp.json handle a server's API secret, and how are remote servers authenticated?
options: Reference the secret via an environment variable, and run /mcp to authenticate remote servers over OAuth
Hard-code the secret in .mcp.json so teammates can use it
Store the secret in the README and disable OAuth
Commit the OAuth token directly into the repo
explain: Reference secrets through env vars so they stay out of git, and authenticate remote servers with OAuth via /mcp. Hard-coding secrets or committing tokens leaks them to everyone with repo access.

kp: Extended thinking: budgets and when to enable
subject: eecs
stem: For which task is enabling extended thinking most worthwhile?
options: A multi-step math proof that requires working through several cases
Looking up a customer's email address by id
Echoing back a value in uppercase
Returning a fixed greeting string
explain: Extended thinking pays off on hard, multi-step reasoning like a proof. Simple retrieval and trivial formatting gain nothing from a reasoning phase and only add cost and latency.

kp: Extended thinking: budgets and when to enable
subject: eecs
stem: A high-volume endpoint just reformats short strings and returns them. Should extended thinking be enabled?
options: No — for simple formatting it adds cost and latency without improving the result
Yes — thinking always improves output quality
Yes — it is required whenever tools are used
Only if the strings are shorter than ten characters
explain: Skip extended thinking for simple formatting, where the reasoning phase buys nothing. Thinking does not always help, is not required for tool use, and the decision is about task difficulty, not string length.

kp: Extended thinking: budgets and when to enable
subject: eecs
stem: What does the budget_tokens setting control, and how is it billed?
options: The maximum length of the thinking phase, billed as output tokens
The maximum length of the user prompt, billed as input tokens
A hard cap on tool calls per turn, billed separately
The cache TTL, billed as cache writes
explain: budget_tokens caps how long the model may think, and thinking tokens are billed as output. It does not limit the prompt, cap tool calls, or set the cache TTL.

kp: Extended thinking: budgets and when to enable
subject: eecs
stem: You are continuing a tool-use conversation whose previous turn used extended thinking. What must you do with the returned thinking blocks?
options: Pass them back unchanged, or the model loses its own reasoning thread
Strip them out to save tokens before continuing
Rewrite them into plain user text
Move them into the system prompt
explain: Thinking blocks must be preserved intact when continuing a tool-use turn so the model keeps its reasoning thread. Stripping, rewriting, or relocating them breaks that continuity.

kp: Extended thinking: budgets and when to enable
subject: eecs
stem: What does extended thinking add to a model's response?
options: An explicit reasoning phase before the final answer
A second independent model that votes on the answer
Automatic retrieval from an external database
A guarantee of valid JSON output
explain: Extended thinking inserts an explicit reasoning phase before the answer. It is not a second voting model, not retrieval, and does not by itself guarantee structured output.

kp: Prefill, stop sequences, and output shaping
subject: eecs
stem: You want the model's reply to be raw JSON with no preamble. How can prefilling the assistant message help?
options: Start the assistant turn with an opening brace so the model continues straight into the JSON object
Add a system rule forbidding all punctuation
Set temperature to zero to force JSON
Increase max_tokens so the JSON fits
explain: Prefilling the assistant turn with an opening brace steers the model directly into JSON and skips preamble. Banning punctuation would break JSON, temperature does not enforce format, and raising max_tokens only affects length.

kp: Prefill, stop sequences, and output shaping
subject: eecs
stem: How does prefilling the start of the assistant message shape the output?
options: The model continues from the text you seed, so a starting brace or role tag locks the format
It appends your text to the very end of the reply
It replaces the system prompt for that turn
It forces the model to call a specific tool
explain: Prefill seeds the beginning of the assistant turn and the model continues from it, steering format. It is not appended at the end, does not replace the system prompt, and forcing a tool is a separate mechanism (tool_choice).

kp: Prefill, stop sequences, and output shaping
subject: eecs
stem: You configure a stop sequence and the model emits it mid-generation. What is reported?
options: stop_reason becomes stop_sequence, and the matched sequence is reported
stop_reason becomes end_turn with no further detail
stop_reason becomes max_tokens
The request errors out with no stop_reason
explain: Hitting a stop sequence sets stop_reason to stop_sequence and reports which sequence matched. It is not end_turn (a natural finish) or max_tokens (truncation), and it does not error.

kp: Prefill, stop sequences, and output shaping
subject: eecs
stem: Extended thinking is enabled and you try to prefill the assistant message. What is the outcome?
options: Prefill is unavailable with extended thinking, since the thinking phase must run first
Prefill overrides and disables the thinking phase
Both apply, with prefill added after thinking as normal
The prefill is moved into the thinking block automatically
explain: Prefill and extended thinking are incompatible because thinking must come before any assistant text, so you cannot pre-seed the reply. Prefill does not disable thinking, they do not combine, and the prefill is not relocated.

kp: Prefill, stop sequences, and output shaping
subject: eecs
stem: Why are prefill plus stop sequences described as a cheap output contract?
options: They shape and bound output without defining or forcing a schema-validated tool
They require a dedicated tool call for every response
They only work when extended thinking is enabled
They validate output against a JSON Schema automatically
explain: Prefill starts the shape and a stop sequence ends it, giving an output contract without the overhead of a forced, schema-validated tool. They need no tool call, do not require thinking, and do not perform schema validation themselves.

kp: Token budgeting and cost engineering
subject: eecs
stem: Which fields does a response's usage block report for cost accounting?
options: input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, and cache_read_input_tokens
Only a single total_tokens number
latency_ms and http_status
prompt_text and completion_text
explain: The usage block reports input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, and cache_read_input_tokens. It is not a single total, and it does not carry latency, status, or the raw text.

kp: Token budgeting and cost engineering
subject: eecs
stem: You want to confirm that prompt caching is actually saving money on a request. Which usage fields tell you?
options: cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens
output_tokens alone
the model id and the request timestamp
the number of tool calls made
explain: The cache_read and cache_creation token fields show how much of the input was served from cache versus written to it. Output tokens, model metadata, and tool-call counts do not reveal cache behavior.

kp: Token budgeting and cost engineering
subject: eecs
stem: On most models, how do output tokens compare in cost to input tokens, and what follows?
options: Output costs roughly five times input, so trimming generated text often saves more than trimming the prompt
Output and input cost the same, so length never matters
Input costs about five times output, so shorten the prompt first
Output is free once the prompt is cached
explain: Output tokens cost roughly 5x input on most models, so cutting what the model generates is often the bigger saving. They are not equal, input is not the dearer side, and caching does not make output free.

kp: Token budgeting and cost engineering
subject: eecs
stem: A long chat gets more expensive each turn even though your latest message is short. Why?
options: Each turn resends the whole history, so input grows linearly as the conversation lengthens
The model charges a flat fee that rises every hour
Output tokens double automatically over time
The context window shrinks and raises the price
explain: Every turn resends the accumulated history, so input tokens grow with conversation length — cache the stable prefix or trim old turns. There is no hourly flat fee, output does not auto-double, and the window size is fixed.

kp: Token budgeting and cost engineering
subject: eecs
stem: You have a simple, high-volume classification step and a rare, hard planning step. How should you assign models and batching to control cost?
options: Run the high-volume step on a smaller Haiku-class model (batched when non-urgent), and reserve a larger model for the hard planning
Use the largest model for both to be safe
Use the smallest model for both regardless of difficulty
Batch the latency-sensitive planning and keep classification synchronous
explain: Right-size the model to the step: a small model for simple high-volume work (batched for about 50% off when non-urgent) and a big model only for genuinely hard reasoning. Using the biggest model for everything wastes money, the smallest for everything fails hard tasks, and batching is wrong for latency-sensitive work.

kp: RAG versus long context: when to retrieve
subject: eecs
stem: A 30-page policy document is queried many times a day and rarely changes. What is the better approach?
options: Keep it in context and cache it, since it fits comfortably and is reused often
Build a RAG pipeline with chunking, embeddings, and ranking
Re-send the full document uncached on every call
Summarize it once and discard the original entirely
explain: A small, frequently reused corpus fits in context and benefits from caching, avoiding retrieval infrastructure. RAG is overkill here, re-sending uncached wastes tokens, and discarding the source risks losing needed detail.

kp: RAG versus long context: when to retrieve
subject: eecs
stem: A knowledge base holds millions of documents that change daily. Long context or retrieval?
options: Retrieval, because the corpus is large and dynamic and cannot fit in context per call
Long context, since stuffing everything in is always simpler
Long context with a one-hour cache on the whole corpus
Neither — send a random sample of documents each call
explain: A large, frequently changing corpus calls for retrieval, fetching only relevant chunks. It cannot fit in context, caching a daily-changing corpus wastes writes, and random sampling would miss the relevant material.

kp: RAG versus long context: when to retrieve
subject: eecs
stem: What is a real drawback of stuffing an entire large corpus into the prompt on every call?
options: You pay for it on every call and focus can degrade at the extremes (needle-in-a-haystack)
It permanently disables tool use
It converts the model to a smaller variant automatically
It guarantees the model ignores the system prompt
explain: Long context is simple but costs tokens each call and can lose focus at the extremes. It does not disable tools, change the model, or make it ignore the system prompt.

kp: RAG versus long context: when to retrieve
subject: eecs
stem: What is the main trade-off you accept by choosing RAG over long context?
options: Added infrastructure — chunking, embeddings, ranking — and a risk of retrieving too little context
Guaranteed higher per-call token cost than long context
The inability to ever cache anything
A hard requirement to use extended thinking
explain: RAG scales large corpora cheaply per call but adds chunking, embedding, and ranking infrastructure and can miss context. It lowers rather than raises per-call cost, does not forbid caching, and does not require extended thinking.

kp: RAG versus long context: when to retrieve
subject: eecs
stem: How does a hybrid approach combine retrieval and long context effectively?
options: Retrieve the relevant chunks, reason over them, and cache stable prefixes to avoid re-sending
Embed the entire corpus into every prompt and skip retrieval
Retrieve randomly and never cache
Replace the model's reasoning with the retriever's ranking score
explain: A hybrid retrieves relevant pieces, reasons over them, and caches stable prefixes so reused content is not re-sent or re-embedded. Embedding everything defeats retrieval, random retrieval without caching is wasteful, and a ranking score does not replace reasoning.
